lessons.title: Even beats: syllable-timed rhythm
lessons.goal: Give every syllable roughly the same length, instead of squashing the unstressed ones like British or American English.

examples.say: What is the plan for today?
examples.means: Each syllable gets its own beat: what-is-the-plan.

lessons.practice: Clap once per syllable while you say the line; keep the claps even.
lessons.listenFor: No swallowed syllables; a steady, bouncing beat.

lessons.title: Retroflex T and D
lessons.goal: Curl the tongue tip back a little for T and D, so 'time' and 'Dadar' sound warm and solid.
lessons.practice: Say 'ta-ta-ta' with the tongue tip touching just behind the ridge, then a little further back.
lessons.listenFor: A firmer, rounder T and D, no puff of air after the T.

lessons.title: V and W, one soft sound
lessons.goal: Many Mumbaikars use one soft sound between V and W, lips close but relaxed.
lessons.practice: Bring the lips close without biting the lower lip, and keep the sound gentle.
lessons.listenFor: A light, even sound for both V and W.

lessons.title: The 'na?' tag
lessons.goal: End a line with 'na?' to make it friendly: asking for agreement, or softening a request.
lessons.practice: Turn three plain requests into friendly ones with 'na?' on the end, rising a little.
lessons.listenFor: A small rise on 'na', warm, not pushy.

lessons.title: Emphasis with 'only' and 'itself'
lessons.goal: Use 'only' and 'itself' to stress a word, the Mumbai way.
lessons.practice: Answer 'When?' three ways with 'only' or 'itself' after the time word.
lessons.listenFor: 'only' or 'itself' straight after the word you're stressing.

lessons.title: Yaar, bhai, ji: who you're talking to
lessons.goal: Pick the right friendly word: 'yaar' for friends, 'bhai' or 'bhaiya' for a stallholder or driver, 'ji' for respect.
lessons.practice: Greet a friend, a chai seller and an aunty, choosing yaar, bhaiya or ji.
lessons.listenFor: The right word for the person, said warmly.
